answers: The ancient Greek theaters were typically built into a hillside, with rows of tiered seating set in a semicircle around the central performance area, the orchestra. Behind the orchestra was a low building called the skênê, which served as a store-room, a dressing-room, and also as a backdrop to the action taking place in the orchestra. Some Greek theatres survive almost intact, the best known being at Epidaurus, by the architect Polykleitos the Younger. Additionally, theatres had specific features like tall arched entrances called parodoi or eisodoi, a two-story skênê with an episkenion, and sometimes a raised speaking place on the orchestra called the logeion.It is important to noete that  the performance space was a simple circular space , the orchestra , where the chorus danced and sang . The orchestra , which had an average diameter of 78 feet , was situated on a flattened terrace at the foot of a hill , the slope of which produced a natural theatron , literally seeing place.

history.content: The theatre of ancient Greece was a significant part of the culture and civic pride in Athens, particularly during the Golden Age of Greek drama in the 5th century BCE. It was formalized after the rebuilding of Athens following the Persian destruction in 480 BCE. The annual Dionysia festival featured competitions in tragedy, comedy, and satyr plays. The theatres had specific features like tall arched entrances called parodoi or eisodoi, a two-story skênê with an episkenion, and sometimes a raised speaking place on the orchestra called the logeion. All tragedies were unique pieces written in honor of Dionysus and played only once until the Hellenistic period. The theatre was used for both public meetings and dramatic performances, with every Greek town having an open-air theatre set in a hillside outside the town. Tragedy and comedy were viewed as completely separate genres with no plays merging aspects of the two.

The festivals associated with the theatre of ancient Greece were significant events that showcased the culture and civic pride of Athens. The City Dionysia, which took place annually, was the most famous of these festivals. It featured competitions in tragedy, comedy, and satyr plays, and was likely organized to foster loyalty among the tribes of Attica. The festival was established around 508 BC, and although no drama texts from the sixth century BC have survived, we know the names of three competitors from that time: Choerilus, Pratinas, and Phrynichus. Each of them is credited with different innovations in the field.

The Hellenistic period, which spanned from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC to the emergence of the Roman Empire in 31 BC, was a time when Greek culture spread throughout the non-Greek world following Alexander's conquests. This period saw a decline in the importance of Greece proper within the Greek-speaking world, with Alexandria and Antioch becoming the new centers of Hellenistic culture. The conquests led to a steady emigration of young and ambitious Greeks to the new Greek empires in the east, resulting in a process of Hellenization and intermixing in regions that had previously been in contact with Greek colonies.
Regarding the theatre of ancient Greece during the Hellenistic period, ithe term " is worth noting that tHellenistic" is a modern invention and did not exist in ancient Greece. However, Hellenistic culture was at its height of world influence during this period, and Hellenism or Philhellenism reached most regions on the frontiers of the Hellenistic kingdoms. Certain Hellenistic influences can be seen in the historical record and material culture of these regions, even if they were not ruled by Greeks or Greek-speaking elites.

Yes. Who were the actors and the directors during the ancient Greek theater?

During the ancient Greek theater, actors were exclusively male and performed in three types of drama: tragedy, comedy, and the satyr play. The first recorded case of a performing actor was Thespis in 534 BC. Male actors playing female roles would wear a wooden structure on their chests and stomachs, and white body stockings under their costumes to make their skin appear fairer. Directors, known as didaskalos, were responsible for overseeing the staging of plays from the writing process to their performance. They often acted in the plays as well, and were also tasked with training the chorus, composing the music, and supervising every aspect of production.
